Mr. Speaker, the second point I wish to raise is one of privilege affecting more the privileges of the house than the personal privileges of a member, but it falls within rule 41 as to decorum in debate. The hon. member for La-belle (Mr. Bourassa), as reported at page 996 of the debates of March 5, said this:
So that a half-witted, blunt or ignorant deputy minister, such as were to be found under various governments and even to this day.
Those are not words which, in the light of what has already been stated to the house, should have been used. May I be permitted to quote from page 4908 of Hansard of May 11, 1933, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), on a question somewhat similar to this, spoke as follows:
Mr. Chairman, I think that ought to be withdrawn. There are certain amenities that should be respected. Has this parliament degenerated to that sort of thing? I just leave it to you, sir. If a member can talk that way about a man who cannot defend him-

self on the floor of this house, about his whiskers, then all I can say is that this parliament has reached a low level.

No member shall speak disrespectfully of His Majesty, nor of any of the royal family; nor of the governor or person administering the government of Canada; nor use offensive words against either house, or against any member thereof. No member may reflect upon any vote of the house, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.
The gentlemen who have been referred to by the hon. member for Labelle, and on behalf of whom the distinguished senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) has just spoken, are not included in this restrictive enumeration. No one of them is His Majesty, no one of them belongs to the royal family, no one of them is the governor or the person administering the government of Canada, no one of them is a member of either house. Therefore the rule by which we all stand, rule 41, does not include those gentlemen. I am in full sympathy with them, but I contend
that what is said by any hon. member, the member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) no more than any other, is not the regulation under which we sit here and debate questions that are submitted to us. I contend that any hon. member can express his own view, but a distinction should be made between any hon. member's personal view, whether he belongs to the cabinet or is a back-bencher, and the standing orders of the house. Such views are not a standing order of the house. This order contains the enumeration by which all members are governed. For the ten years that I have been a member here no hon. member has attacked the governor, no one has attacked His Majesty, they all observe this rule. The hon. member for Labelle, for whom I have great respect, enjoys freedom of speech. I believe that a member of the House of Commons is entitled-
Oh, oh.

Sir, I will ask the Sergeant-at-Arms to put out of the house the asses that are braying so loudly. When I say that I do not wish to cast any reflection upon any hon. member of the house. Sir, what I say is, that the rules of the house are contained in this green book. They are the law of this chamber. No member may do anything which is not permitted by those rules; when he does you can rightly call him to order, he has to stand by your ruling. I have great respect for opinions expressed by hon. members, other than by banging their desks; when a member shows his intelligence by reason and argument I have great respect for his views; but I do not govern myself by, and no one can compel me to be governed by the views expressed by an hon. member personally. All we have to do is to stand by the rules of the house. In conclusion my contention is-

I am just concluding. I
say that we are not bound by what is said by any hon. member of this house. We are bound by the rules of the house, and according to those rules the hon. gentleman, I am very sorry to say, is out of order in this case.

I would like to get some information from the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion). He may not be able to give it to-day but might give it to-morrow. It is with regard to the pooling of trains between Quebec and Montreal which is announced to take place on the 10th instant. It is a peculiar pooling, in that all the Canadian National trains are taken away and all the Canadian Pacific trains remain. This will cause much inconvenience to the travelling public, and still more to the employees of the Canadian National Railways. I would like to have full information as to the conditions under which this pooling has been agreed to, in order that we may discuss it with full knowledge of the facts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon.
gentleman said, I do not know the facts at the moment and cannot answer fully. I shall do so as soon as I get them. But let me say one thing now; that is that where trains are pooled and what my hon. friend calls the Canadian Pacific trains continue to run, the fact that the time of a pool train corresponds with the time table of the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National matters not, because pooling means that the returns are pooled, so that it is as fair to one railway company as the other. I mention this so there will be no misunderstanding.
[Mr. Speaker. 1
As to questions relating to hours, with which I presume my hon. friend is chiefly concerned, I shall make inquiry and endeavour to give a full explanation.

Are the employees also
pooled? Are Canadian National employees going to work on Canadian Pacific trains? Because only Canadian Pacific trains are being retained, and they are 'being operated on the Canadian Pacific line.

As far as the employees
are concerned, we put a clause in last year's bill which the railways claim they are living up to, providing that whenever any pooling is done every effort shall be made to be perfectly fair to the employees of both railways. In regard to the specific instance my hon. friend refers to I cannot give a particular answer, but the railway managements are endeavouring throughout the country, wherever there is pooling of shops or trains, to balance the employees of one railway with the employees of the other. However, I will give the hon. member a fuller reply as soon as I look into it.

As my hon. friend knows, as Minister of Railways I have nothing whatever to do with the pooling of these trains; this is done under an arrangement between the managements of the two companies for the purposes of economy. I did have a statement which I received this morning, which unfortunately I did not bring with me, in regard to the pooling between Ottawa and Toronto and Montreal and Toronto, showing that they claimed a saving of something like a million passenger train miles per annum. They usually estimate the cost at SI a mile, so they figure they are making a very great saving. However, I merely emphasize the fact that neither the government nor myself, as minister, has anything to do with the pooling

The house resumed from Monday, March 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cahan for the second reading of Bill No. 4, respect-ting the bureau for translations and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Chevrier.

Mr. Speaker, I stated, last evening, that the bill under discussion, has not the import which the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), seem to have given it. Far from being an additional guarantee of the rights of the French language, it is of a nature to restrict it by leaving to the bureau created by this bill the care of interpreting the guarantees given to our constitution. Besides, it takes away from the different departments the bilingual character which must be theirs under the present system.
If it is a fact, as has been said, that section 133 of the British North America Act limits the compulsory use of the French language to the printing of the house records and of the statutes, I fail to see how the proposed legislation shall fundamentally place the two languages on an equal footing. If the intention be really to create that equality of standing, as far as the two languages are concerned, in the various departments of the public ser-

1208	COMMONS
Translations Bureau-Mr. Jean
vice, it can be done in a far safer way than through the centralization of translating staffs. Let us provide for the appointment of bilingual officers in every department. Such efficiency, production and economy as might be secured under the latter plan are surely more apparent than in the indefinite cooperation provided for in sections 3 and 4 of the bill now before the house. If it is desired to ensure the simultaneous publication of the house records in both languages, would it not-the only way to achieve the end in view-be better to leave the translators in direct contact with the ministers and officials entrusted with the preparation of such documents, as is the case at the present time.
I am willing to admit that to a certain extent there is room for improvement in the present system, but the conditions could not be improved through the crowding of the translators into one department. For instance, the French edition of the Hansard is being issued two or three days late. Why? Because of the fact that the translators have to wait for the English text proofs from the Printing Bureau. Should the typewritten copy, as it is being prepared, be handed over to the translating staffs, the French edition of the Hansard could be made available practically at the same time as the English edition. The same could be done, if desired, in connection with all other publications. But such is not the object aimed at by the hon. Secretary of State in introducing this legislation. The object in view may be found in his explanatory notes of the bill:
It is believed that the organization and' administration of the proposed bureau^ for translations will result in improved efficiency and a considerable saving of public funds.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that the debates translators, as well as the other translators generally could discharge their duties in a more efficient manner than they do at the present time, and I fail to see how economy would result from the proposed bureau for translations.
Efficiency and economy can only be obtained through the competency of the translators, and whatever system is put in force, better results in every respect will be secured with qualified men and the cost of translation will be accordingly less.
On the other hand, there was no demand from anywhere for the proposed legislation. The majority of those who are more directly affected by the bill, are opposed to it. The French press in this country has declared itself against it. Most of the French speaking members in this house are also opposed to the measure. I even suspect that, at the 
start, our honourable friends from the province of Quebec who sit on the other side of the house, were not in favour of the proposed plan. Why such an insistance to have it carried out and how are we to account, Mr. Speaker, for that distorted construction which is being placed on the bill? Has the hon. Secretary of State stated at any time that the end he had in view when introducing the bill was to recognize the principle of an equality of status for both languages, and does the bill itself contain a single provision the intent or letter of which warrants such an inference? Not a single word in the whole bill justifies that construction being placed on it.
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to enter into a discussion of the bill in its details as well of the unfairness it involves as far as the translators are concerned. The point has already been fully covered and it is needless for me to go over the same ground again. But I am of the opinion that the arguments put forward in support of the bill have not been proven and that the objections raised against it have not been refuted. Our friends on the other side of the house have taken us to task because we failed to offer to them any advice as to the position they should take. Should they be willing to take a friendly word of advice from their friends on this side of the house, I may say to them in concluding: Do not press this bill to the end, or it might prove a boomerang against yourselves.

Translations Bureau-Mr. Parent
similar to the administration of any business concern. When a reduction of certain expenses or of certain fixed charges is desired, appropriate measures must be taken. I do not wish to criticize the hon. Secretary of State for having paid special attention to that point, because I know that in a time of depression like this, any government or business concern must try to cut down expenditure. But how does the Secretary of State propose to attain this object? It has been said that useless expenditure to the amount of hundreds of thousands of dollars has resulted from errors in translation, which had to be corrected on the galley proofs sent back by the King's Printer for revision. These galley proofs have to 'be revised a second time, and so as to avoid this useless expenditure or loss of money, it is now proposed to centralize the translators, in the hope of bringing an improvement. The hon. Secretary of State claims that the present system is responsible for the errors and omissions of the past. I shall not attempt to find who was responsible for the errors complained of; errors may hap,pen anywhere, nothing is perfect in this world. Even admitting that those errors may have cost the amount mentioned by the hon. Secretary of State, should he not, before presenting such a bill, consult the heads of the different departments and ascertain if all the translators have done their duty, if certain departments are not short of translators, and finally if at certain times of the year some translators are not overworked. Would it not have been possible to hold an investigation so as to find out in what departments the wohk is not done as it should be, and to try some corrective measures for six months, for one year, or even for two years, before bringing down in this house a bill which antagonizes a large section of the population of our country? If the complaints are justified, a little investigation would have removed the cause of the trouble.
I am surprised that no report whatever should have been presented to the house, and that we are not told of any efforts made to remedy the conditions and to remove the cause of the errors found in the work of the translators of the various departments. Instead, we are told: "We want to centralize the translators in order to economize public funds."
There shall be a bureau for translators, according to the terms of the bill. The hon. Secretary of State says that the bureau shall be divided in two branches, but there is not a word to that effect in the bill. There shall be a bureau; that is all. Where shall
IMr Parent.]
that bureau be located? Will it be on Sussex street, on Wellington street, a mile away from the centre of the city? Where is it going to be? We do not hear a word about that. One thing is certain; everybody knows, and it will be an extraordinary spectacle when the law shall come into force, to see messengers running around the city of Ottawa-
On bicycles?

-on bicycles, on street cars, walking, motoring, with bundles of papers, with state documents, with departmental files concerning the smuggling of narcotics, the arrest of high placed individuals, or with other papers of the highest importance. And do you think that no errors could happen during the handling of all those documents? I have every confidence in our staff of messengers, 'but some of them may be weak; such is human nature and it cannot be changed. All those documents shall first be taken from the departmental files and registered by an official, then the chief of the department will hand them to a messenger, who will start on his journey through the streets of the city-

And the
country-side.

-in the
direction of the bureau for translations. There, he will deliver the papers which will be registered on an index card by the receiving clerk, who will stamp the hour and date of reception, and inscribe the nature of the documents received for translation. The chief of the bureau must then take the document and hand it to one of the translators. Then the work of translation begins. When the work is completed the translated text must be submitted for revision. The revision over, the document comes back to the chief once more and then starts travelling again-
The same messenger, with his bicycle.

The same messenger riding a bicycle or driving a car will bring it back to where it started from, the official files, whence it will be forwarded to the King's Printer who, mayhap, will receive it rather late. I have counted seven formal stages through which the document must necessarily pass.
A genuine "pigeon hole".

And it is estimated that each department,-there are

Translations Bureau-Mr. Parent
47 of them in the service,-will handle an average of twenty documents each and every day. Multiply 47 by 20, then multiply that result by 7, and you get the fabulous number of more than 5,000 manipulations that these documents will have to undergo every day under a centralized translation service such as that proposed by bill No. 4.
The translation marathon.

Without mentioning the danger of certain indiscretions, of involuntary losses or omissions, on the part of the messengers. But there is more than that. Can one admit for a single instant that documents of the highest importance should be temporarily withdrawn from the official files and allowed to leave the premises of the different departments?
A very serious matter, indeed.
And what would happen if at that very moment, for some important reason, or some matter of emergency, a neighbouring department should request the instant return of a document so withdrawn?
The Secretary of State did not foresee that.

You can
imagine the frantic search that would result to find the wanted document among the two or three thousand that would be in the hands of the translation bureau.
A game of "hide-and-seek".

All these
things must be considered when it is sought to establish a centralized organization like that proposed by the hon. Secretary of State under bill No. 4.
Mr. Speaker, the centralization of the translation service means the centralization of our translators. A translator, it has been said repeatedly and I say it again, is a specialist. I will add that his work calls for professional qualifications. Time was, when we wanted any document translated, official or otherwise, we used to enlist the services of some University graduate-
Or some amanuensis in Montreal.

-to have that translation done. For years now the translators of the various departments, byi dint of constant application and study, have
become specialists in the terminology of the subject dealt with in their respective departments. Moreover the professional character of the translators' work has been duly recognized and a technological association founded in Ottawa. Why? For better training of the young men who graduate from our universities and who thus have the inestimable advantage of self-improvement and of specialization along one or more lines, under the guidance of the technological association. The latter is made up of translators who have had years and years of experience in translation work. A number of works have been published, and as time goes on their number will be added to, by translators whose purpose is to acquaint posterity with the fact that to be a translator does not imply the mere understanding of one language or another, or the stringing together of words from one language to another, or the spoken use of one or more languages: the translator must grasp the full meaning of a given text and reproduce in the other tongue the very intention and the thought the given text is meant to convey.
Are you in favour of the status quo?
Of the status quo, such as it is? Yes. With improvements? Yes; but notMong the lines set out in bill 4.
Hear, hear.

We must realize, Mr. Speaker, and my hon. friend knows it, that no such change as that suggested in the bill can be undertaken after an experience lasting sixty years: If the centralization of the translation services were at all feasible, the thing would have been done before now. An investigation was held and committees appointed to study the proposed system; in every instance the suggestion was rejected. And with very good reason: If you take every translator in the departments, or ten of them from ten different departments, and throw them together with all their notes and encyclopedias, where will you put them? Will they be grouped in a large class room, as in their school days? Will they all be placed under the watchful eye of the superintendent? No, Mr. Speaker, a translator needs no supervision, because it might happen that being a specialist in certain subjects, he would know more about them than his chief or, as w*

often hear, he would know more than his teacher. If all the translators are grouped in the same building, or in the same room, they will not be able to work with the same efficiency as if they were in separate offices, and they will have to work under worse conditions than in the past. Why not leave them in their respective departments where they have access to the other documents essential to the proper interpretation of the texts they will be called upon to translate?
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): Hear, hear.

[DOT] If they are centralized, every time they will need some document a messenger will have to be sent for it. In certain cases, fifteen days may elapse before they get the papers they need. It is impracticable.
That never occurred to any one.
Lots of things have not occurred to these gentlemen, and if the Secretary of State had taken the trouble of making the slighest investigation-
If he had known his business.

-he would have found that the objections*raised in this house are sufficient to justify the six months' hoist moved by the honourable member for Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, as very few members have discussed this bill, I think that I should be allowed more than forty minutes, but I shall conclude my remarks. I have not yet mentioned a group of men who occupy an important place on the "staff" of the official translators.
Oh.

My hon.
friend has the hiccups.
We will have a game of croquet.

I am speaking of the translators of the House of Commons and of the Senate. In the course of his explanation of the bill, the hon. Secretary of State said that he intends to have a separate branch for the translators of the House of Commons and of the Senate. Why did the sponsor of the bill make that declaration so readily? Because, after listening to the arguments on this point, the Secretary of State came to the conclusion that they are well taken and that the bill will not detach the officials of the House of Commons and of the Senate to place
[Mr Parent.]
them in a department. Why? The House of Commons and the Senate are two representative bodies created by the British North America Act and their officials are responsible to the two houses and not to a department. That cannot and must not be changed, they are a distinct body under the terms of the British North America Act and they must remain officials of the houses of parliament and not be placed under the Secretary of State.

What part of the British
North America Act is the hon. member referring to?

I am referring to section
133 of the British North America Act by which I say the translators are members of the staffs of both houses of parliament, the Commons and the Senate. They are vested with rights by the spelling of the law of that article of confederation. Therefore I say that it is impossible that a group from the staffs of both houses of parliament should be separated from those staffs and be put under a minister of the crown. There is no staff of the House of Commons or of the Senate that is directed and supervised by a minister of the crown. The staffs are the staffs of the House of Commons and of the Senate.

But the hon. gentleman
knows well that other services of the House of Commons and of the Senate are performed by departments which are under the direction and control of ministers of the crown.

But the minister surely
will not put on the same footing the services of the translators because the translators are in a sense the voice of the representatives of the people of the whole country. We are not going to set their service side by side with that of the employees of a department. Certainly not. I absolutely object that the translators of the House of Commons should be considered on the same footing as employees of any staff outside the House or the Senate coming under the Civil Service Act.

I understand the argument.
Thank you.

That is what I wanted to
point out.
(Translation):	It would greatly decrease
the prerogatives of the House and Senate, if the group of officials, placed by the Confederation Act under the two chambers, were removed. We must bear in mind that we represent the people. The hon. ministers opposite, who are held responsible for the ad-

Translations Bureau-Mr. Hackett
ministration of this country, are aware that these officials translate their speeches. What do they translate? They translate the voice of the representatives of the people, yet, it is the desire to lower their status, to remove them and place them behind a departmental screen known as a Bureau for Translations. I protest. I do so for the honour of my country, on behalf of our fathers who signed the confederation pact. When this act was signed by the representatives of Great Britain and those of Upper and Lower Canada, the spirit of this pact stipulated that both English and French should be on the same footing in both houses of parliament, and that it was an official duty for the translators to translate from one language to the other and vice versa, the words spoken by the representatives of the people in this country. I am absolutely opposed to any steps, being taken to establish a difference between these two languages and lower the standing of this group of translators of the house and senate.
I have just stated, sir, that this bill could not be enacted without doing a grave injustice to certain translators assigned to the translation of the debates of the house. The work is of a special and technical nature more than any other, because the subjects discussed here are more complicated than those met in the correspondence of the various departments. I, therefore, state that parliament would make a mistake in forsaking the authority over the translators and its privileges. There is a restriction embodied in this bill but there is also an open door so that, in the future, this bill may serve as an excuse to say to the French Canadian people: By this bill, you have agreed to a kind of compromise. You had, by virtue of the British North America Act acquired rights, which had been adhered to since 1867. By virtue of this bill No. 4, you have agreed to a kind of compromise, you have agreed to discuss the questions as to the extent of these rights and what they embody I state, sir, that it is untimely to discuss our rights. I shall therefore oppose this bill by voting for the amendment.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): Mr. Speaker, I do not entertain all the fears of the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Parent) in connection with this bill. I have read it carefully and I see in it nothing but an administrative measure. However, it touches one of those topics which arouse the susceptibilities of a substantial group in this house. There are many such topics and several such groups and I need not go further back than the beginning of this session to
find an instance where the mention of a subject. however innocently intended, aroused the feeling and support of other groups.
All the arguments for and against the bill have been so broadly canvassed that I do not think I can add very much thereto. However, there is one point to which I should like to address a few remarks. I am vitally interested in good translations and I think that the house as a whole is likewise interested. At the proper time, I should like to see those translators who translate the debates of this house and of the Senate placed on a different footing from the other translators. Nothing is more difficult to translate than colloquial language. It is racy and frequently tinged with slang which, after all, is language in the process of gestation. The translators of the debates of this house and the Senate work under great pressure; they work long hours and cannot during the period of their service enlarge their acquaintance with languages and their evolution. I was down there a couple of weeks ago to see if there were any printed in French, and was told that they would' not be ready for four or five months. Tf they are not ready for four or five months is it any use to have them at all When we come here at the beginning of the session we cannot get a French report of any kind.
In 1906 the Hon. T. C. Casgrain complained again, and is reported in Hansard of 1906, volume 2, page 3323 as follows:
Although a number, of bills are on the order paper for second time, they are not printed in French. I do not wish to put any obstacle in the way seeing that the session is well advanced, however, I do not want this to be a precedent.

Translations Bureau-Mr. Gagnon
In a debate in this House of Commons in 1907 the hon. member for Labelle, the same hon. member who represents Labelle to-day, is reported in Hansard of 1906-07, volume 2, page 3663, as follows:
The ground of complaint is that though the quality of both languages has been conceded by all governments and by the house, the French translation department is treated as an unimportant department. If we had an adequate number of translators for the work of translating both the debates of the house and bills and other documents published under the authority of this parliament, there would not be any such delays.
And then, later on:
We receive letters almost every day from our constituents asking us when they can get a certain document in French. The French version of the debates are often from two to three weeks behind, and those of bills and other public documents are often a month or more. I have known of a delay of six months before we could get the French translations of certain public documents. Almost every year there is an extraordinary case. For example, the records of committees of this house have to be translated and printed.
I will be fair enough to admit that in 1910 Sir Wilfrid Laurier was alive to the situation and saw that the question of translation was discussed before a special committee of this house. A committee studied the matter, following which Mr. Frechette, to whose report reference has been made by hon. gentlemen opposite, was sent abroad in order to study the matter. The committee of 1910 studied the matter of centralization of translation, but as Mr. Frechette reported in the negative no action was taken. I have quoted the extracts from Hansard to show that notwithstanding complaints which had been sent by public bodies, by French newspapers and by many public corporations in the province of Quebec and elsewhere we are not much more advanced than we were forty or fifty years ago. Of course, there have been some slight improvements with respect to the translation of debates of the house. With respect to the translation of documents of departments the situation is still so imperfect that French translations of committee reports and reports of departments are sometimes published six months and more after the issue of the English copies. Is it not imperative, sir, I seriously ask you, that appropriate measures should be taken to achieve a considerable and definite improvement? The proposed bill will put a stop to such an undesirable state of things. When this bill becomes law the members of parliament who have done nothing during the long years of parliament to improve the situation, and who may have been tempted or are now tempted sometimes, 74726-78
no matter to which political party they belong, to make political capital out of the late production of French translations must admit that when the French copies are delivered at the same time as the English copies the whole of our French population will be very much better satisfied and will be grateful to members of parliament for this new legislation. There is no doubt, I humbly submit, that this bill ought to receive the unanimous support of all the French members of this house irrespective of party affiliations.
The hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) and the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Dubois), for whom I have a great admiration, have spoken of the disapproval of this legislation by a certain number of French newspapers of Quebec and Ontario. That is unfortunately true, but after having read all these articles carefully wTe cannot do other than draw the conclusion that the writers have been unduly apprehensive or that they have been misled by some of the translators or their friends. They argue as if it were true that the translators would be dismissed or their numbers considerably lessened on the passing of this bill. I sincerely believe that with the new bureau for translations in operation the number of translators will have to be increased instead of being decreased. The economy that the government is endeavouring to bring about does not consist in the reduction of salaries of translators or in their retirement or dismissal, but in the stopping of that obnoxious and ridiculous practice of having two, and sometimes three or four galley proofs prepared before the typewritten document is finally printed and published. The Secretary of State has said, and has not been contradicted, that last year $75,000 was misspent in the revising, resetting and reprinting of documents which should have been corrected, not on the printer's galley proof, but on the typewritten document written by the translators.

The hon. gentleman has made reference to the amount that it costs for the correction of galley proofs of the French translations. Does he know how much it costs for the correction of the English galley proofs?
The hon. gentleman cannot expect that I can answer a question like that. He has only to read the speech of the Secretary of State where he will find all the details set out.

He did not refer to that.

1224	COMMONS
Translations Bureau-Mr. Gagnon
Mr. GAGNO'N: Is it not true that more translators could be employed if we could save $75,000 a year and bring about the reforms that we ask for. The attitude of the men at the printing bureau who are fathers of families and are receiving small wages compared with the translators ought to interest parliament as much as the attitude of the translators. The Secretary of State has explained that because the service of translation is improperly and imperfectly organized he has been obliged to dispense with many French-Canadian printers who in December last had no means to pay for food, fuel and shelter. The creation of the new bureau will enable the government to economize and keep these people in their jobs. Need I recall to hon. gentlemen opposite that printers of French are French-Canadians just as much as the translators of this house or of the departments? The poor printers may be less learned in the sciences than the translators. They may have fewer friends among the newspaper men, because a great number of the translators are old journalists, but on the other hand I respectfully submit that the case of the poor printers is just as deserving of sympathy as that of any other civil servant who painfully and honestly performs his duty and earns his daily bread.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) has given a somewhat exaggerated picture of the operations of the proposed bureau. Speaking at page 1021 of Hansard he said:
Suppose this department is organized and a head is appointed to supervise all translations coming therefrom. The Secretary of State has a document, to be translated and he calls up the bureau for translations and asks for a man. Possibly the subject relates to agriculture, and of course the bureau, following railroad rules, first in first out, in order to divide up the work, so that no one will be overloaded and everyone will have the same proportion, sends out a man who probably has taken two years at university in the study of medicine. This man knows all the medical terms, and he is called upon to translate something relating entirely to agriculture. There will certainly be a good' many technical terms quite unknown to him, and he accordingly produces an erroneous translation. What will be the state of affairs if the minister happens to be a gentleman who is acquainted with one language only? Vice sersa, suppose the Minister of Health calls for a translator to give him a translation of something dealing with medical questions. He calls up the bureau and as translators 5, 6 and 7 are out, No. 8 is assigned to this work. He is quite familiar with agricultural terms but he knows nothing whatever about the terms used in medicine. Could anything be more ridiculous?

Does the hon. member for Sherbrooke seriously believe that the bureau for translations will function in the ridiculous way which he described in a rather humorous fashion? Surely he must credit the chief of the bureau with some common sense. The hon. member has had much experience in the lumber and papermaking business. What would he say if the foreman of one of hia mills would indifferently call a chemist to do the work of an engineer or a chauffeur to do the work of a paper-maker? He would think his foreman had gone crazy. Why would the future chief of the bureau for translations use less common sense and good judgment in the management of the bureau than the foreman of one of my hon. friend's lumber or paper mills?
Other hon. gentlemen opposite have described the pitiful fate of the translators and have depicted the future bureau as being a place where the translators will be pressed together like sardines under the terrible eye of a supervisor who will impose silence upon them just as a schoolmaster does upon his school children. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite where in the bill do they find even the suggestion of such ridiculous proposals which, as a matter of fact, they can find only in their own imagination. The chief of the bureau for translations will have to be a man thoroughly conversant with the French and English languages. Very likely he will be a French-Canadian, and eventually one of the translators will become chief of the bureau. Does any hon. member seriously contend that the future chief of the bureau will be a despot or autocrat who will think only of cutting the translators' throats? Some hon. gentlemen smile, but nevertheless that is the kind of argument that we have read in some of the newspapers and which has been used by some hon. gentlemen opposite in opposing this bill.
Many hon. gentlemen have referred to the report of Mr. Achille Frechette, who in 1910 was chief of translation of the House of Commons, and who declared himself against the centralization of translation. I have nothing to say against that gentleman, but it seems to me that many changes have taken place since 1910. At that time radio was nonexistent and aeroplanes were very imperfect. Bleriot had only recently been hailed as a great man for crossing the English channel. Do hon. gentlemen seriously believe that because a suggestion was considered impracticable in 1910 it could not. be acted upon in a practical fashion in 1934? The translators will not lose their liberty under the

Translations Bureau-Mr. Marcil
provisions of this bill. Those who are experts in certain lines will continue to do the work for which they have special training and experience. Those who are experts in agriculture will not be called upon to translate matters relating to mineralogy. The Secretary of State has stated in unequivocal terms that the translators of the House of Commons will remain under the jurisdiction and control of that house. The vacation which these translators use for historical and literary studies may be preserved. A section of the Civil Service Act protects them in that respect. I am surprised that hon. members opposite who have been so free in picturing French Canadian Conservative members as traitors to the French language have not invoked that special legislation which has so far protected the translators and ensured them a long and restful vacation.
This is not the time and place to attempt to improve this legislation; it should be done when it is brought before the committee which has been specially constituted to study the bill and make a report to the house. Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to have acquired lately a great knowledge of translation matters and I invite them to appear before that committee and suggest any remedies they may have in mind. In order that the translators may have assurance with respect to their salaries, I suggest that a special clause be inserted to guarantee that these salaries shall not be decreased and that the privileges which they have enjoyed so far shall be maintained. The committee will have to bear in mind that the translators assigned to the different departments sometimes work until only five o'clock in the afternoon, whereas the translators connected with the House of Commons and the Senate sometimes work very late into the night; so much so, that after a long and strenuous session these translators find themselves exhausted and in need of a good rest. I should be pleased to recommend that their vacations be as long as possible and I am sure that this phase of the matter will be considered carefully and sympathetically.

It would be a new
bill with those changes introduced; we have to vote on the bill as it is at present.

We have voted on bills
before which have gone to a committee and come back in a state hardly recognizable. Why should it be otherwise with this legislation?

We hope so.
74726-78J

The hon. member for
Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) has had a great many years of experience and he should know that the procedure followed by the committee considering this bill will be the same as that which has been followed ever since parliament has been sitting.
The strongest criticism against this bill is that it will have the effect of reducing the importance and influence of the French language. No one has attempted to prove that the creating of a new bureau will have such michievous results. On the contrary, instead of translations being left entirely to the discretion and good will of the heads of departments, henceforward they will be under the direction of a chief of translations appointed by order in council or statute who, by his culture, training and functions, will be interested in maintaining, defending and improving the status of the French language. The definite pronouncement made last evening by the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) should go far to reassure those who are unduly apprehensive in this regard. Should this bill pass, for the first time since confederation the translation of departmental reports and public documents will be upon a permanent statutory basis. The hon. member for Ottawa has referred to section 133 of the British North America Act. Many hon. gentlemen opposite invoke this section more often when in opposition than when in power. I am sure Le Droit, which attacked the view presented in the speech of the hon. member for Labelle, will be interested in knowing what Senator Belcourt said about this in 1912 when speaking at the Congres de la langue frangais a Quebec.

The hon. gentleman has spoken the allotted period of forty minutes.
Hon. CHARLES MARClIL (Bonaventure): Mr. Speaker, I have been very much interested in the reminiscences of the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon). I was a member of this house when complaints were made by his predecessors from Montmorency and Dorchester. I have been hearing these complaints all during the thirty-four years I have been a member. I was Speaker of the House in 1910 when Mr. Frechette was instructed to visit Belgium and Switzerland to ascertain the best method of carrying on translations. Belgium is a bilingual country, French and Walloon being the official languages, while Switzerland is a trilingual country, with German, Italian and French. During the thirty-four years I have been a member there has
1226	COMMONS
Translations Bureau-Mr. Marcil
been constant complaint of the lateness and delay in the publication of documents in French. The older members of the house will remember these complaints. The translators have always contended that the delay was due to the printing bureau. Canada is English by an immense majority, but it seems to have been forgotten that both languages were put upon an equal footing at confederation. In this country French is just as official as English. The statutes are not translated; they are supposed to be originally French. All documents should be printed simultaneously in both languages.
What would happen in this house if French members were to speak nothing but French, if they were to move amendments in French, raise their points of order in French, make their motions in French and ignore the English language completely? Where would we be? Could the business of this house be carried on? Those who are familiar with the work of this house will know what would happen. The French members have always made it a point to learn the English language, and I think this is greatly to their credit. I have known some of the most brilliant members of this house who, in their early manhood, knew hardly any English at all. They later became masters of the English language and they set a fine example to the English speaking members. I am glad to know that to-day it is becoming fashionable throughout Canada to learn French. If a Canadian wants to realize the importance of this language all he has to do is to go to Europe; unless he knows French he is lost entirely on the continent. English is the business language all over the world, but French is the language of the day in Belgium, in Switzerland and everywhere on the continent, as the minister himself will admit.
I am sorry I have only a few minutes and cannot fully discuss the bill, but the hon. member for Dorchester has discussed a bill which is not before the house; that is the unfortunate part of it. The Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) is a distinguished gentleman, an outstanding Canadian, a man who represents in this house a constituency which is largely French-Canadian, and it cannot be conceived that his object in bringing before the house such a measure is to deprive the French people of their constitutional rights, which, if this bill as it stands passes, they will not possess hereafter, but which they possess by virtue of the constitution which made confederation possible. We all know that without Quebec there would not have been confederation; Quebec was the connecting link between the maritime

provinces and Ontario. Those who are interested in the subject need only read the debates of confederation, the words of Sir. John A. Macdonald, Sir George Etienne Cartier, and others to realize that both languages are official; that Canadians, whether French or English, are equal in the eyes of the law and that in this parliament the French and English languages are equal. Of course this is not so in a number of the provinces, but it is fast becoming so. As people become more learned and know the advantages of two languages, they appreciate the value of a knowledge of French. I can remember some distinguished men who have entered this house, among whom I could mention two or three prime ministers, who have consulted me as to the best books to read in order to learn French rapidly and who admitted afterwards that they were sorry they were handicapped by not having begun earlier in life to learn the French language.
The question now before the house is: How should we give satisfaction to the two or three million French people living in Canada? If we are going to spend $250,000 a year to translate, as under the law we must, the translation should be done in accordance with the best traditions so that we shall get value for our money and the people will have these publications in their proper season. Fancy the English speaking members of the house having to wait for three days for the English Hansard, or sometimes six months or more for reports of some of the departments! That is the difficulty with which we have to contend. Similar complaints to those voiced by Thomas Chase Casgrain, former member for Montmorency, Jean Baptiste Morin, former member for Dorchester, and others, who sat here thirty-five years ago are rampant to-day. Almost every day w'e have people write us to send them such and such a report in the French language. AVhen we reply that we cannot do so because the report is not printed, they ask: When will it be printed? If the members of the house and of the committee which is going to study this bill want to know the real facts of the case, they should just summon the press gallery representatives of the French newspapers of Canada and find out how they are treated in the way of translation, how they are handicapped, how all documents, announcements and pronouncements are invariably thrown at them in the English language and they must translate them on the spur of the moment otherwise the French population of Canada, reading those newspapers, will be deprived of the advantage which they should possess.

Buffalo-Fort Erie Bridge Company
I understand the minister intends amending this bill very materially and making probably two sections of this new bureau of translation.
It is not necessary to amend the bill in order to accomplish that.
I understand he intends to amend the bill if amendments suggested are shown to be advantageous.
I can assure the hon. gentleman in that regard.

The minister knows the
difficulty of translation of parliamentary language; it is a language of its own. In parliamentary language there are forms and expressions which are not found in any other. Those who read the debates of the French House of Representatives will find that a large number of our expressions are unknown in the parliamentary language of France and that it is only with time, experience and study that a man becomes competent to translate parliamentary language. Therefore, if we have a staff specially trained in that work, it would be very unfortunate to disperse them, to put them to other work after they have become expert in the work they are at present doing. The same thing applies in the case of every other department. For instance, a man has spent years making a special study of mining, agriculture, finance, if you like, or any other branch and he is put at a moment's notice at some other work. The invariable result is that the work he will do will not be as good as that to which he is accustomed. I am sure the minister is willing under the circumstances that this bill should be materially amended, and he should remove any suspicion of doubt that the French people of this dominion are being unfairly treated in this matter. It is the duty of every member of the House of Commons to work to bring about a cementing together of and a better understanding between the people of this country, because therein lies its salvation.

I entirely agree with the
hon. member.

Minorities, as the minister
knows, are always very sensitive in regard ^ to their rights, and if there is the least suspicion that they are going to be deprived of any of the advantages they now enjoy, a great deal of harm will be done. In the meantime I shall have to vote for the six months' hoist, but if, when the bill comes back from the committee for third reading, it is materially improved, I have an open mind and I shall dead with it then on its merits.

subtopic: BUFFALO AND FORT ERIE PUBLIC BRIDGE COMPANY
speechtext:
It is not my intention at the moment to oppose the second reading of this bill, but I would like to call the attention of the house to it, particularly the attention of those members who may be on the private bills committee. There seems to be some misapprehension in the minds of hon. members, and also in the mind of the public, as to the position we put ourselves in when we vote for or against the second reading of a private bill. Those of us who were in the house when the Georgian Bay canal bill was discussed will recall the situation that arose then. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) was then leading the opposition. The Prime Minister of the day propounded the view that when a private bill came up for second reading it got that second reading as a matter of course, unless the house was opposed to the principle of the bill. The hon. member for South Wellington accepted that view, but there was a difference of opinion between the two hon. gentlemen, the Prime Minister of the day contending that the principle of that bill was the construction of a canal, while the hon. member for South Wellington contended that it was the construction of the canal by private interests. So we had a sham fight in the house for three or four weeks, and finally the bill went to the private bills committee and was killed.
I make these remarks because of a report that appears in the Montreal Witness from its parliamentary correspondent referring to a private bill that was before this house a few days ago, providing for the establishment of a company to loan money. The remark is this:
The five Liberals voting for the bill were Hon. W. R. Motherwell, Hon. P. J. Veniot, J. L. Ilsley, F. W. Gershaw and Ross Gray, even after he had spoken against it.
I want to point out that it is not at all inconsistent for an hon. member to speak against a bill and yet vote that it be allowed to go before the private bills committee where the measure can be discussed on its merits and where those promoting the bill may have a chance to present their views. Private in-

dividuals certainly have a right to come to parliament and present their views to the private bills committee.
As I said, it is not my intention to oppose the second reading of this bilk As far as I understand the bill at the moment, I am opposed to it, but I conceive that it is quite possible for me to be opposed to it and yet be willing that it should go to the private bills committee to be discussed on its merits. I think it desirable that there be a full attendance at the committee so that we may hear the matter discussed from all points of view. Certainly if some of the objections that occur to me at the moment are not removed I shall oppose the bill not only in committee but when it comes back to the house.

Bonds and property to be tax exempt. speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to my hon. friends opposite, this afternoon, discussing the stand taken by the press of this country on this bill No. 4; I wondered whether their mind had not been influenced by editorials which we have read of late. It might be interesting to know who organized and spread the campaign undertaken by a number of French Canadian newspapers, even before this measure was introduced in the house.
We did not intend, sir, to carry on a long debate over this bill. We had even hoped after the masterful statement made by the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan), followed by the convincing speech of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), who is unquestionably an expert on the subject, that the house would have adopted the second reading and referred the bill to a committee.
However, our hon. friends on your left, sir, put up a concentrated opposition; however, I do not doubt it is genuine. But judging from the speeches delivered this afternoon, I cannot do otherwise than state that this opposition is directed by the general staff of the Liberal party and aims at influencing public opinion.
I listened, to-day, to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Ferland), who stated that this bill had been so draughted that it could be interpreted one way in one province and another way in another. Judging from the standard of speeches delivered, this afternoon and for some time past, my opinion is, that they were delivered in view of influencing public opinion and intended as political propaganda. I have, sir, not only read-
. Mr. VENIOT: I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman has just made a statement in French, with regard to the speeches made on this side of the house this afternoon, attributing a motive to the speakers on this side. He says that in those speeches hon. members on this side wish to influence the public for election purposes. He has no right to make a statement of that sort.

Translations Bureau-Mr. Duranleau

I humbly submit, Mr. Speaker, that the point of order is absolutely uncalled for, because the Minister of Marine is entitled to say that the speeches made on the other side of the house were intended as political capital. There is nothing unparliamentary in that.
Will the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) be good enough to elaborate the point of order? I did not quite comprehend it.

The Minister of Marine, in his remarks, said he was convinced that the members on this side, in opposing the bill, were making their speeches with the main object of influencing the public for election purposes. He is attributing a motive to us, and he cannot do so.

I have listened to the words uttered by the Minister of Marine, and I submit that they are absolutely in conformity with parliamentary procedure. No one was mentioned; it was simply an allusion to the fact that on the other side of the house * speeches were made with such and such a motive, merely a political motive.

On the point of order, I suggest in all frankness that a great many speeches made on all sides of the house are for the purpose of influencing public opinion. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if the Minister of Marine is ruled out of order for making such a statement, most of us, when we make speeches in this house, in which we endeavour to influence public opinion by explaining our position, would be ruled out of order.

I do not suggest that we are not allowed to make speeches to influence public opinion. My point is that no hon. member has a right to stand up in this house and say to any other member, "You are making 'that speech to influence the public for political purposes." That is attributing a motive, and under the rules of the house no motive may be attributed.
Not an improper motive.
I cannot believe that the hon. member for Gloucester is serious in raising the point of order.

I was stating, a moment ago, that a campaign had been cleverly organized, even before this bill was introduced in the house. And when I read in a newspaper that this bill was directed against French influence in this country, I greatly regretted that the author of this article had summarily set aside the
statement and the clear, sound precise and genuine explanations made in the house by the hon. Secretary of State. Moreover, that he had summarily disregarded a career well fulfilled, in the course of which, the sponsor of this bill, the hon. Secretary of State, has always given proof of fairness towards all races and languages in this country and shown much sympathy towards his fellow-citizens speaking the French language-no one can deny this fact-often at the expense of his popularity. Secretary of State has always taken towards all races of this country. Is the hon. minister aware that the Secretary of State has no translator in his department and that he does not speak the French language.
We shall have some.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Glancing over the speeches made by the opposition and reading the articles published in newspapers, we must conclude that the opposition to this measure can only come from an inexact or even false interpretation, to some extent, of the provisions embodied in it. After all, if we consider these speeches and articles, there are only four objections to the bill; first, it would deprive this house of one of its most cherished privileges; secondly, it would result in lowering the value and efficiency of the translation in the various departments; thirdly, it would make the position of translators in this country more precarious; fourthly, it would endanger the status of the French language in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, all these points have been fully discussed since the opening of this debate. I want to be as brief as possible, but I must admit that the first objection does not impress me very much. The house is the ' sole guardian of its own privileges, but it is never prevented to waive them from time to time in the interest of a more efficient conduct of public affairs. These privileges, however, are but a sequel to our duties as mem-i bers and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that our primordial duty is to ensure, through sane and proper legislation for the country and its people, the wise conduct of public affairs.

Should our rights and duties, in the fulfilling of this task, become conflicting, and if the ones have to supersede the others, who is the member of this house who would dare maintain that our duties ought to give precedence or bow to our privileges? My hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Bouchard) says that there are many "ifs". If he listened to the speeches delivered on the other side of the house, he must have realized that all the arguments of our hon. friends opposite are based on "ifs".
Mr. Speaker, the second objection to this bill is that it will result in lowering the value and efficiency of translation in all departments. That is a serious objection, because it strikes the very principle of the bill; but I wonder, Mr. iSpeaker, where one can find either in the spirit or in the letter of this bill, any proof of the claims of our hon. friends opposite. In order to judge, you must first ask yourself whether the present system is giving all the results that you are entitled to expect from it and whether it works out efficiently and rapidly enough. It is an extraordinary thing that although our hon. friends made long and frequent speeches and carried on a splendid effort, not one of them cared to suggest any improvement that might be brought into the present system. It is surprising that it is the press of the country that complained most frequently and most violently about the present system, about the documents being published in one language only and also about the delay in the translation. I may add, Mr. Speaker, that- very often these complaints were fully justified. Therefore, it is strange that when we are about to remedy that condition, when we wish to improve the translation system through a bill that has been thought out and studied during many months by men who,
I believe, know something about translation, [DOT] it is strange indeed that these same newspapers, even before the bill was submitted to the House', protested most strongly against the improvements which we wanted to bring into the present system.
Is there one member in this house who will maintain that the present system is perfect?
Nothing id perfect in this world.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Will you say that there is no place in the present system for improvement, that there is no need to change it, considerably if necessary, in order to make it fully efficient? For it is the French race, the French section of this country that has had and still has to complain about the present system of translation. It *was for us to complain, because, quite often, the French editions were useless owing to the tardiness of the translation.
What we want to secure with this measure is precisely a more elaborate translation of all official public documents, a translation which might not be any better than it is now -because I do not wish to criticize our translators or the translation that has been done up to now-but which will be carried out in the shortest possible delay.

There is
nothing to that effect in the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The
idea of centralization seems to terrify our hon. friends of the opposition and especially the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier). In his speech the other day, he depicted the continuous parade of " Baby-Austins " and messengers hurrying to and fro between the central bureau for translations and the different departments. More than that: he attempted to show the superintendent distributing work to his 87 or 88 subalterns and ordering, for instance, the specialist in geology to translate the report of the investigation on milk production and distribution. Better still: at certain times, my hon. friend for Ottawa seemed to think that the different specialized translators would leave all their knowledge at the door of the central bureau, which is also the fruit of his imagination, because no central bureau is mentioned in the bill; that question is left entirely in the hands of the superintendent or of the minister in charge of the department.

I said
nothing of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
This
is a reasonable deduction from my hon. friend's remarks. He even went so far as to exhume the report made to this house in 1910, by Mr. Acbille Frechette, and which has since been quoted so often. That report had been made at the request of the Internal Economy Commission of this house following a special survey trip to Belgium and Switzerland. That report shows that Mr. MARCH 6, 1934	1231
Translations Bureau-Mr. Duranleau
Frechette proposed Belgium as a model. But, Mr. Speaker, what were the conditions in Belgium, in 1910, according to Mr. Frechette? This is what he says on this subject on page 4 of his report:
Each of the different departments has its own translation staff, except the department of Foreign Affairs, the occasional translation business of which is done by the very comprehensive staff of the Ministere des Chemins de fer, Postes, Telegraphes et Marine, counting sixteen members. Beside the work for the foreign affairs, this staff is also expected to do that of the Universal Postal Union, the international conventions and the proceedings of the peace conference. The Finance department has one translator proper; science and fine arts, two; interior and agriculture, two; war, three; justice, three; colonies, two; public works, one.
Briefly, 16 translators were centralized in one department and were at the same time doing the work of two or three other departments, while 14 others were scattered in the remaining departments. If I am not badly mistaken, even at such a remote period, as has been said this afternoon, we can discern the beginning of a system of centralization.
But will such a centralization be carried as far as the hon. member for Ottawa and some of his colleagues of the opposition seem to think? As I said a few moments ago, nothing in the bill justifies such a thought or supposition, and in his illuminative explanation the Secretary of State proved the contrary. In fact, nothing in this bill will prevent a translator, specialized or not, who has enough work for every day of the year, to remain in his present office while being subject to the supervision of the superintendent; that would entirely conform to the letter and to the spirit of the act. I say, Mr. Speaker, that nothing in this bill provides for the grouping in one office or in one building of all the translators, including those of the House of Commons and of the Senate. And I have been pleased to hear the Secretary of State declare that a special department would be organized for the translators of the House of Commons and of the Senate. The technical and specialized translators shall remain so under the new system resulting from this bill. Is it because they would be under a unified control, or under a minister responsible to this house, that the translators would cease to be employed as specialists? The contrary is evident, Mr. Speaker.
The hon. members of the opposition should do the Secretary of State the honour to believe that the superintendent would not be such a fool as to trust the translation of laws to a specialist in geology. The only conclusion which we may draw from the
speeches of my hon. friends is that the translators are going to be thrown helter-skelter in the different centralized offices. The superintendent, and the minister in charge also, will be acquainted with the competence and the special qualifications of each translator, and will distribute the work accordingly. In the first place, the object of this bill is to ensure a fair distribution of the work.
Hear! hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The
hon. Secretary of State has proved in black and white that such is not the case presently.

Rather
in black.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
-and not one single member of the opposition has been able to say so. It is plain, too, that at the present time all the translators are not treated in the same way, both as regards promotion and as regards the work itself. Another thing we want,

and I feel convinced that the bill now before the house offers a means of obtaining it-is the translation of a greater number of documents from the different departments.
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): Hear, hear.

A greater

At the present time the number of documents to be translated is left to the discretion of the various deputy-ministers. Under the bill a chief will be appointed who will see to it that all public documents, from all the departments, will be translated into both languages.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): Will he be given more authority than the deputy-minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Our
translation service will be under a minister responsible to the people and to this house. As things are, Mr. Speaker, if we have any fault to find with the translation, we must complain to \ our Honour, and you have no responsibility in the matter; when the translating is under a responsible minister we will at least be able to obtain a hearing for our complaints and have things set to rights. I say that is extremely important for the French element in this country.

As I said before, Mr. Speaker, what we want most of all is to ensure a service sufficiently prompt to permit of the simultaneous publication, in both languages, of all reports, bulletins and documents of immediate interest that a delay in translation might cause to become absolutely worthless, such as the French reports on the cattle industry, on dairy products and divers other farm produce, mentioned in "Le Devoir' of February 20th, over the signature of Mr. Albert Rioux.

We
obtained simultaneous publication by getting away from centralization.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: It is by having a competent superintendent who will see to it that the translating is done efficiently and rapidly, in all the departments-
Will the hon. minister allow me a question?

I'll make another one.

speechtext: I have only forty minutes at my disposal. The hon. member will have a chance to speak on the main motion; if he so wishes, he can then produce his arguments.
He can also appear before the committee.
Read the article by Mr. Rioux.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The
fear exists, apparently, that the present bill will make it difficult, if not impossible, to recruit and to train specialized translators. This is another statement based on a supposition that is entirely gratuitous, that is, that the superintendent of the bureau will have no consideration for the proficiency of each translator, and that the men will be continually transferred, constantly shifted around from one place to another, as it has been alleged. It is absolutely unreasonable to presume any such thing. At the present time our foremost experts have assistants who are being trained under them. Do the hon. members of the opposition really believe that when the service is brought under one head this excellent practice will disappear? What is there to justify any supposition of that kind? After all one is bound to recognize that the minister

who will be made responsible for this service, the Civil Service Commission and the General Superintendent, who wiM be called upon to organize it with him, without being endowed with genius, will at least have ordinary intelligence and ordinary judgment.
Well-deserved praise has been given the initiative and the zeal shown by a number of translators who are forever on the look-out for technical information to perfect themselves in their art, who prepare dictionaries and technological manuals of all kinds, and who have established a system of reference-files where they store up their acquired data and their discoveries. Putting the service under one head will prevent, what has sometimes happened in the past, the loss of the fruits of such persevering study and research, and will facilitate the creation of a sort of library, of a. card-index system, that the effort of every translator will make more complete every day, and which will be an inexhaustible mine of information. In the past certain translators took all their notes with them when they left the department. Under a direction such as we intend to establish for this service, nothing of that sort can occur.
They will simply laugh at the very idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say it again, the intention is not to pile up the translators into one large office, nor under one roof, but to secure uniformity, as well as equalize results, in order to obtain greater production and higher efficiency in the translation service.
Once more, Mr. Speaker, it is indeed strange that, in all the speeches delivered against the proposal by the hon. members sitting at your left, and after which the sound argument put forward by the hon. Secretary of State and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), remains unimpaired, in ail these speeches, do I say, one would look in vain for the assertion that the existing system is faultless, that it fully meets with the requirements of the conditions at the present time as well as the legitimate demands of the public at large. But, when the hon. Secretary of State, who has given considerable time to the matter, introduces a bill drafted after due reflection and meant to put an end to legitimate causes of complaint, we are at once confronted with a mass onslaught from within the ranks of the opposition^ specially from the members representing my own province

Quite so. Hear, hear!
