speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: [DOT]-the very one which, in the past, has had to suffer the most as a result of the delays we are endeavouring to eliminate.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
From
the very outset, in this debate, we have been told time and again that translation is a complicated art requiring a full knowledge of languages and even, quite frequently, a great sum of learning. We oftentimes hear hon. members extoll the high competency and the unceasing efforts of our translators, a tribute to which I am only too pleased to associate myself with as much sincerity as any one else, if not in so many words; we have heard the commendation of decentralization so ardently advocated, would it seem, in 1910, by Mr. Frechette who, after all, only approached the problem in so far as the debates of this house, the sessional papers and the legislation were concerned, a fact which detracts to a singular degree from the value of the conclusions it is sought to draw from his report. It must be pointed out that, the author of this report referred incidentally to the various departments of the government, for he had been appointed by the Commissioners of Internal Economy of this house for the sole purpose of reporting on the translation service of the house and of the Senate, a fact which, in my opinion, considerably lessens the importance of that report in this debate.
As I was saying at the outset, I read every one of the speeches delivered by my hon. friends; I have listened to those delivered this afternoon and I was wondering where, in these various speeches, could be found a single reason, a constructive argument warranting the continuation of a system which led to the deplorable state of affairs so clearly set forth by my hon. friend the Secretary of State and the hon. member for Labelle.

You could
not have read my speech for I have not spoken yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The
other day, I heard, and then read, the speech delivered by the hon. member for Kamour-aska (Mr. Bouchard). He himself found fault with the present system. In fact, did he not complain of the translation of the treaty on the St. Lawrence ship canal? Therefore, it is to be inferred that my hon. friends admit that a change is necessary in the translation service.
It is because it was translated without charge by a friend of the Secretary of State.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: At least, so far as this bill is concerned, the change we are making is commendable.

It is not
the result of translation and these changes are not contained in the bill now before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My
hon. friend shall be given the opportunity of giving all the explanations he may desire to give at a later date.
He is the specialist in interruptions.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: To the hon. members on the other side of the house we ask: Why such a strong opposition to this proposed legislation? The answer which we get is that it shall entail the elimination of comparatively high positions and lower some translator chiefs to the rank of subalterns. Mr. Speaker, I already stated, and I feel bound to say again, how I hold in high esteem the translators generally. I am pleased to pay tribute to their ability; I know that most of them, are not of the kind who would be content with getting through their actual work in a more or less indifferent manner; on the contrary, they are constantly delving into research work, following closely the evolution of languages, familiarizing themselves with recent discoveries and inventions, in order to add to their technical vocabulary-

The hon.
minister differs with the hon. member for Labelle.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I am
giving my personal opinion; I agree with the hon. member for Labelle when he says that this measure is calculated to improve considerably the present conditions.
If you agree with him, he must be wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for Temiscouata.

He said
it just the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
We are told, Mr. Speaker, that our translators were deeply moved by the announcement of this measure.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): And rightly
so.

Translations Bureau-Mr. Duranleau

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: They are uneasy and fear wholesale dismissals. Where will you find in the bill that is now before us and especially in the principle of this bill, the least thing to fear for these competent and hard working translators?

If there are
dismissals, you will he held responsible for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
They
will certainly not complain in the future when the work will be more equally divided, in order that one translator may not be called any more to translate 1,719 pages within the year, and another only a few pages.
Then did our translators and those who, in this house and outside, mean to hasten to their rescue, read carefully paragraph 7 of section 3 which promises plenty of work, much more than they had in the past, therefore surely preventing a reduction of the translating staff. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, this section contains the sanction of a principle that has been perhaps imperfectly recognized in section 133 of the Confederation Act, And, protected as they are by the Civil Service Act, how could they fear any lowering in rank involving a reduction of salary? Again, it is not a concentration camp for translators that the measure is calculated to establish, but an intelligent centralization and even a rather mitigated one, in practice, of the various services, with the sole object to ensure a greater measure of efficiency. I do not see what could prevent the chiefs from remaining chiefs, because the superintendent to be appointed, as it was already stated, will not claim any relationship to the great man referred to the other day, who is known in history as Pic de la Mirandole. Our superintendent will not claim to be possessed of the learning and special knowledge of our chief translators. Therefore he will have chiefs in the various translation branches.
So much the better.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
His duty, if I understand the bill aright, will consist mainly in co-ordinating and distributing the work, with a view to having it carried out promptly, but without meaning to so teach anything to the specialists and technicians under him.
Having always in mind the interest of the translators, there is another aspect of the question that our hon. friends seem to have missed. Do they fully realize, that the present

system is liable to depreciate the value of the translation service, especially for the French language? With the tardiness and considerable delays that it allows, the present system will finally make the translation of many documents useless, because by being so delayed they have lost all their value.

It is not
the translators' fault.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation):	It is not the
translators' fault; it is that of the departments.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
It is
the fault of the present system, because the French edition of reports and journals of present interest are published only several days and even weeks after the English edition.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation):	Whose fault
is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Then
what happens in such a case? The ratepayer, merchant, manufacturer or farmer, who needs it immediately, takes the habit of reading it in the English text and therefore does not ask for the French edition. Our hon. friends opposite should realize that when the deputy ministers see the French editions being piled up in the cellars, they cease having these documents translated, and that is at the expense of our race and of the French language.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): But it is their own fault, because the English original is sent too late to the translators.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friend will have the opportunity to answer; he might even be called before the committee.

But he won't go.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): I won't go? I shall go if I am called.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If I understood correctly some of my hon. friends this afternoon, they have raised a weak opposition to the bill now before the house-I am speaking of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil). He even suggested that it would be a good idea to refer the bill to a committee where it could be amended.
It certainly does need amendments.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My hon. friends will be called upon to make suggestions.

Translations Bureau-Mr. Cardin
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): I suggest that you call before the committee the translators whom you have accused when they have no way of defending themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I concur in the opinion of those who think that a measure such as the bill now before the house may be discussed without resorting to dishonest or disloyal arguments, and without inflaming public opinion. It is wrong to say that the present bill concerns only the French-speaking members and the people of the province of Quebec. It should interest as well all other members of the House of Commons, because translation is not only made from English into French, but also from French into English.
This bill rests on two principles which have been clearly defined by the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan). By the way, I hope he understands that all those who oppose the bill have not the least intention of casting reflections on his personality, his character, his sincerity and his broad-mindedness. We have known him in public as well as in private life; we respect him as a private citizen as well as a statesman, and we have the highest consideration for his professional and legal ability. Therefore, this bill should be discussed in the light of the reasons and principles to which he has given expression in the course of his explanations. What are they? They are neither a safe-guard for the rights of the French language, nor a reinforcement of the position it occupies in the parliament of the country. It is childish to say so. Here are his reasons: economy and greater efficiency in translation. They are the only two arguments brought forward by the Secretary of State, and they are also the inspiration of this bill.
The translation of documents costs too much, and the printing costs too much because the translation is not ready in time. Those are the true reasons. It is useless to look elsewhere in trying to justify the position taken by the government, or in the desire of crowning with a halo the Secretary of State and the government for this so-called recognition of the principle of the rights of the French language. This bill adds nothing whatever to the rights of the French language, which shall continue to exist even if this bill be rejected or withdrawn. It does, not add one iota to the rights of the French language, as we have them to-day. In my humble opinion, I prefer the present recognition of the rights of the French language in the several departments to the recognition which would come only from a central bureau of translations.
Economy? Shall the enactment of the present bill result in any saving? Not at all. From the discussion and the answers given to the questions from this side of the house by the hon. members sitting at the right of the Speaker, an increase in the cost must be anticipated.
My hon. friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) has just said that a greater number of books and documents will be translated than in the past. This should be more expensive. I have no complaint on that ground. But it is a flat denial of the argument of the Secretary of State who wants economy. Further, every member of this house knows by experience that centralization, in all spheres of human activity, has not resulted in economy. Generally speaking, the methods of administration have become worse when centralization has been introduced in the public services. It has resulted in poorer service at a higher cost. The centralization of all .the translators of the public service, or of certain translators will produce no saving in the cost of government. We shall see a great number of officials in charge of this new bureau of translations, an increase in the number of translators and supervisors, a new staff of employees who will be going forward and backward between the bureau, the different departments and the House of Commons; in other words a general increase in the number of employees. If there are, to-day, translators who are remiss in the accomplishment of their duty, there will be men directing this department who will earn their salary less than the translators earn it to-day: they will act as overseers.
The hon. Secretary of State said: It may very well be that a complete centralization will not be brought about in the one place, the one building; we may establish certain departments in certain government buildings, small staffs where a certain number of translators, accustomed to a particular line of work, will be retained under the direction of a special official. It is evident that this will incur additional expense. The more there are of these branch translation offices the heavier will be the appropriations voted to defray the cost of the translation service. Therefore, from the standpoint of economy, let us not deceive ourselves; it is childish to pretend that any saving may result from a like reorganization of the service.
Will there be an improvement in the translation? I doubt it. WThen instead of being under several heads who control them or who are supposed to control them, the translators will be brought together in one building, under the direction of one chief, it is quite
1236	COMMONS
Translations Bureau-Mr. Cardin
possible that there may be just as much neglect as the translators are accused of today.
I think it is unjust to say that the translators attached to the different departments are not useful and do not do their duty. Among the translators-I make no claim to knowing them all; but I do know some of them-are some who are officials of sterling worth who render valuable service to their respective departments. In this service as in every other may be found certain civil servants who are not up to standard; but if we look into all the branches of the public service we find the same faults that the present bill seeks to remedy.
The translation will be not one whit better than it is to-day. It may well be, and I am quite prepared to admit it, that my experience is rather limited with respect to the translating done in the House of Commons. If I understand the matter aright that is where the evil lies that the hon. Secretary of State is trying to eradicate. Then why not restrict the reform to the translators of the House of Commons and of the Senate, adopt measures suitable to this category of translation, appoint a translator as chief of the service, and give him the requisite authority to direct the employees under his jurisdiction. Why not leave the translation in the different departments entirely independent of that done in the House of Commons and the Senate; in this way, as the former Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) so well pointed out, the translators at present attached to the various departments would remain in line for promotion in their respective departments. If these employees of the several departments, Frenchspeaking employees mostly, are organized into a central bureau or placed under a new director, they will lose their chance of promotion, will no longer be able to try for the position of departmental chief or of assistant deputy minister. Oh, I know quite well that the hon. Secretary of State told us beforehand that these men will be entitled to promotion in the translation bureau. But there the chances of promotion will be meagre indeed. When the hon. Secretary of State will have the power, under this bill once it becomes law, to order the transfer of a translator in the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) to the central bureau of translations, because of his exceptional proficiency, that translator will have to leave the work he has been doing in the Marine department and come under the direction of the translation bureau where 
he will be barred from all prospects of promotion, save the opportunities, few and far between, afforded by the bureau itself. He will be deprived of the advantages he enjoys at present in the department, where he can aspire to any position in that Department of Marine. You have there a serious consequence of this measure, brought to the attention of the house by the former Postmaster General and other hon. members; an argument that remains unanswered by our friends on the other side.
My very good friend, the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) has not answered it; my very good friend the hon. Minister of Marine has not answered it; and, foreseeing the objections, the hon. Secretary of State did not answer it either. He insisted that the translator could be promoted within the translation bureau. But promotion within the translation bureau would not have the same importance, far from it, as promotion in the different departments of the public service, as things are to-day. There you have a disadvantage; the employee will have fewer opportunities for promotion if this bill, in its present form, becomes law. In future those who enter the government service through the translation bureau will be deprived of their chances of rising to higher positions in our civil service.
Efficiency! I doubt that the proposed system, once adopted, will ensure greater efficiency. But if certain evils exist, if certain employees are remiss in their duty, why not deal with them in the translation service as they are dealt with throughout the government departments? Does the hon. Minister of Marine expect us to believe that if a translator, in his department, does not do his work properly but loafs away his time, that my hon. friend has not the necessary authority to make this man attend to business as he should? Why does the hon. minister wish to throw this responsibility on the superintendent of the Translation Bureau or on the hon. Secretary of State?
It may be that when we ourselves were administering the affairs of this country certain unpalatable things occurred and that we might be charged with neglect in certain instances. I do not agree with those who claim that the administration we set up was absolutely above reproach: like the present government, ours was made up of human beings, with the usual measure of human frailty. I say in all sincerity that if I were to be called once more to-day to administer the affairs of the Department of Marine there are certain things I would not go about in just the same way. There is always room for im-

Translations Bureau-Mr. Cardin
provement in any situation; but I maintain that each minister should not be relieved of his due responsibility. The minister who has a translator directly under his authority is better fitted to make that translator toe the mark than would be any official appointed to preside over the destinies of a Translation Bureau. I repeat:	When errors or faults
crop up, correct them; indolent and careless employees, people who fail to give proper attention to the tasks assigned them, should be dismissed. When in any department certain employees are found who are not properly fitted for their work, do you reform that department, do you abolish it and merge it with some other department? Is it fair to solve the problem in such a roundabout way, when you can strike directly at the root of all the trouble? Once more I say: let the faults be corrected, you have all the authority you need.
I cannot accept the eloquent plea made by the hon. Secretary of State in explaining his bill, when he stated that he had to go outside the service to have a translation made of the Speech from the Throne.

A pretty
weak argument.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have difficulty in imagining the hon. Secretary of State, with the English copy of the speech from the throne in his hand, going from one department to another looking for some one to translate it, and coming back to his own office without having found a translator. It may be that from a technical viewpoint, and with microscopic hairsplitting, one may conclude that, technically speaking, certain employees of the House of Commons, of the Senate and of the different departments, might refuse to do this work. Well, I am very humble if I compare myself to the hon. Secretary of State, I am quite a small man, intellectually as well as physically, compared to him. But, were I in his place, I would like to see the translator, employed by a government of which I was a member, who would have told me he refused to translate the speech from the throne. It appears to me that the government cannot very well be proud of t>he fact that they must publicly declare: We had to go outside the translation service to have the speech from the throne translated because we could not find a translator to do this work. It is certainly not an argument in favour of the bill; and if I were the Secretary of State I would not have advanced a reason of that sort in a public document. I am convinced that if the hon.
Secretary of State and the members of the government had applied to the officials of the House of Commons they would have found somebody to do this translation. Furthermore, if they had applied to some of the secretaries of the present ministers they would have found five or six only too glad to translate the speech from the throne, and their translation would have been of a high order. They may pass a resolution, if they so wish, asking, nay instructing the Prime Minister by a majority of the chamber that they do not wish any further recommendations to be made.

That privilege lies in this House of Commons. But I do entreat those who are concerned about the maintenance of our institutions, who love our constitutional liberties and realize the extent to which they rest upon the exercise of

If I may interpret freely the words of the right hon. Prime Minister, I would earnestly urge the hon. members opposite to abstain from concluding that the House of Commons, by its vote on the bill now being considered, can divest itself of its prerogatives which are in respect of constitutional liberties secured as a result of the struggles waged by our ancestors.

To use the words, sir, of one of the greatest geniuses the world has known, I say to hon. gentlemen opposite: Canada has her eyes on you, she expects you to redeem your pledges, she awaits your help. May I ask hon. gentlemen opposite whether they were as frank in 1930? Why did hon. gentlemen not mention that the distress which had made its first appearance in 1929, was the result of a world wide crisis? I do not wish to appeal to race prejudices and my hon. friend the Solicitor General has neither the right to do so. Whatever may be the races which form the population of this country, I am certain that the monopoly of justice, equity, truth and of all that is good in the human heart is not centred in one race, in particular. It does not belong more to the Canadians of French origin than to the Canadians of English or Scotch origin. It is in the heart of all well thinking citizens -and they are the majority. I place more trust, sir, in what is good in my fellow-citizens, whatever religion or race they belong to, than in any useless law text. To use, in closing my remarks, the thought of one of the greatest writers of modern France, may I say:
What matters whether justice is embedded in the law, if it is not deep in the heart. And if the heart is bad of what good is the equity which governs the law. Keep the compass and the level away from the crafty surveyor, for with well adjusted instruments, he will apportion unfairly. As long as men are misers and cruel, they will interpret the kindest laws cruelly and will despoil their brothers with words of love.
Mr. Speaker, the law counts for little. It is the spirit of the law, the spirit born from feelings existing in the heart which counts. I shall close my remarks by stating that the whole of this discussion is futile; we have thrown away considerable money uselessly; we have wasted too much time in the discussion of this bill, and were I permitted to make a suggestion to the government, I would say: Set aside all these measures, do not endeavour to decoy the people with such humbug as that of the inquiry on the spread of prices. The government endeavours to becloud public opinion with investigations such as the committee on agriculture held on milk, last year. I ask the hon. Minister of Marine, as well as all his colleagues: Where is there a farmer who sells his milk at a higher price since this inquiry was held?
